metadata.title: The historical evolution of European medical device regulation: from fragmented national systems to a harmonized supranational framework
metadata.description: This review traces European medical device regulation from fragmented national systems to the harmonized framework established by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) and Regulation (EU) 2017/746 (IVDR). It examines the pre-harmonization period (1957–1985), characterized by diverse national approaches in Western and Eastern Europe, including Bulgaria's regulatory development during the post-communist transition. It explores the New Approach to technical harmonization (1985), the directive era (1990–2000), and how regulatory crises—including the Guidant pacemaker failures, the DePuy ASR hip prosthesis scandal, and the PIP breast implant fraud—served as stress tests confirming the necessity of reforms. Special attention is given to emerging challenges from artificial intelligence in medical devices following the adoption of the AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689).

metadata.title: eurlex-builder: a configurable Python pipeline for EU legislative datasets
metadata.description: eurlex-builder turns the EUR-Lex / Cellar corpus into provision-level Parquet tables for quantitative research. It fetches directives, regulations, decisions, and communications, extracts text at configurable granularity (article, numbered paragraph, or lettered point) across EUR-Lex's heterogeneous document formats, collects metadata and inter-document relations, and includes guarded Opus-MT translation for non-English documents. Output is one DuckDB file plus four Parquet tables. The package accompanies Seidl and Kosti (2026), "Mapping Europe's Digital Acquis: A Granular History of EU Digital Policymaking".

metadata.title: MultiLegalPile: A 689GB Multilingual Legal Corpus
metadata.description: Large, high-quality datasets are crucial for training Large Language Models (LLMs). However, so far, there are few datasets available for specialized critical domains such as law and the available ones are often only for the English language. We curate and release MultiLegalPile, a 689GB corpus in 24 languages from 17 jurisdictions. The MultiLegalPile corpus, which includes diverse legal data sources with varying licenses, allows for pretraining NLP models under fair use, with more permissive licenses for the Eurlex Resources and Legal mC4 subsets. We pretrain two RoBERTa models and one Longformer multilingually, and 24 monolingual models on each of the language-specific subsets and evaluate them on LEXTREME. Additionally, we evaluate the English and multilingual models on LexGLUE. Our multilingual models set a new SotA on LEXTREME and our English models on LexGLUE. We release the dataset, the trained models, and all of the code under the most open possible licenses.

metadata.title: Biometrics Data Space: Ensuring Trustworthy and Secure Data Exchange for Suspect Identification
metadata.description: Concerns about privacy protection, ethics, and the urgency to adhere to EU regulations for personal data protection are increasing as digital biometric technologies are widely being adopted in order to improve the accuracy of the identification and verification processes. This paper proposes the formation of a Biometrics Data Space, a trusted ecosystem that is based on the Data Spaces technology and offers secure sharing and exchange capabilities of biometric data in potential use cases, such as foreign Law Enforcement Agencies (LEAs) and forensic agencies, with an aim to facilitate the process of reliable identification of the suspects. The suggested identification framework incorporates Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PETs), such as homomorphic encryption, to address data protection concerns. Moreover, Large-Scale Data Indexing is applied to the biometric data to provide a fast and efficient comparison o fag iven facial image with ones stored in owners' local premises and without disclosing any personal information during the search and match process. Furthermore, automated access rights control is implemented by Blockchain Smart Contracts that are integrated into the Biomet-rics Data Space framework. The main objective of the suggested framework is to offer a reliable and automated identification system that ensures trust, data sovereignty, interoperability, and robust data protection.

metadata.title: Dataset_Supply security narratives have dominated EU raw materials policy, while demand reduction has been sidelined_Herdlitschka et al. (2026)
metadata.description:
The research sample consists of policy documents from four key stakeholder groups involved in EU raw materials policymaking: civil society, political institutions, research, and industry. These groups were identified based on their active engagement in public consultations and participation in relevant committees, such as the Raw Materials Supply Group and the High-Level Steering Group. We collected a total of 183 policy documents from these stakeholders, representing their contributions to EU raw materials debates between 2000 and 2024. 

Data types detail: Policy documents, four stakeholder groups

creators.name: Herdlitschka, Theresa
creators.affiliation: UPOL

metadata.method: To construct the dataset, we first conducted an initial targeted document search using platforms tailored to each stakeholder group. For civil society and industry stakeholders, we primarily used Google to locate relevant materials published by these groups. For political institutions, we gathered documents from the EUR-Lex information system and other official EU publication services. Academic contributions were identified through the Scopus database. Following this initial search, we employed a snowballing approach by reviewing references, citations, and links within the collected documents to expand the dataset further.

metadata.title: Przemysł 5.0: Powrót człowieka, kreatywna automatyzacja bez hakowania
metadata.description: Przejście od Przemysłu 4.0 do Przemysłu 5.0 nie jest już rewolucją technologiczną, lecz fundamentalną ewolucją mentalną i architektoniczną. Industry 4.0, zorientowane na technocentryzm, traktowało człowieka jako najsłabsze ogniwo procesu, które należy wyeliminować. Przemysł 5.0 redefiniuje tę relację, wprowadzając paradygmat antropocentryzmu (Human-Centric), rezyliencji oraz zrównoważonego rozwoju. Szybka automatyzacja Industry 4.0 obiecywała fabryki bez ludzi, ale przyniosła sztywne linie produkcyjne, podatne na przestoje i cyberataki. Przemysł 5.0 ma naprawiać ten błąd, przesuwając inżyniera z pozycji nadzorcy do roli inżyniera procesów sztucznej inteligencji lub architekta procesów „myślących”. Techniczna anatomia nowej ery zaczyna się od sterowników PLC z systemami kontenerowymi i napędów przemiennikowych z kompleksową diagnostyką sygnałów i zaawansowaną analityką prądowo-momentową po cyberbezpieczeństwo sieci przemysłowych. Te rozwiązania i nowoczesny sprzęt mają rozwijać ludzką kreatywność, aby to człowiek zbudował tarczę cyfrową, odporną na zagrożenia współczesnego Przemysłu. W pierwszej kolejności dokonajmy inżynieryjnej analizy błędów poprzedniej ery oraz zweryfikujmy oczekiwania, które definiują architekturę nowych współczesnych fabryk.

metadata.title: Surplus Food, Food Waste and Discards Quantification and Management Practices in Food Transformation Industry. Survey Data and Descriptive Statistics
metadata.description: A significant challenge faced by the food industry worldwide is food waste (Somlai, 2022). Global food waste accounts for 931 million tons along the food supply chain every year (UNEP, 2021). To tackle the issue and support effective prevention and reduction strategies the first step is to be aware of the amount of waste generated (Corrado et al., 2018). Primary data collection is vital for effective food waste management, yet the understanding of its generation and management at the firm level is lacking (Xue et al., 2017). Collecting more data and improving how data are used is essential for tackling societal, climate, and environment-related challenges (European Commission, 2020). However, as stated by Silva et al. (2019), despite recognizing the importance of measuring and assessing food waste data, companies still lack cohesive and applicable measures in this regard. In addition, there is still a relative absence of empirical research on food waste measurement and management practices adopted by firms since investigating this topic is considered a complex task (Corrado et al., 2019). Indeed, as stated by Baquero et al. (2023), obtaining accurate data on food waste is challenging due to various factors such as improper recording, lack of standardized measurement methods, and the diversity of sources. This paper answers this urgent need, by describing and presenting a novel dataset on food surplus and food waste measurement and management practices adopted in the Italian food transformation industry, included quantitative data on surplus and waste production. Data have been collected through a large-scale survey involving a sample of 1,812 firms (22% of the reference universe) stratified over 3 size classes (small, medium and large firms), 10 product categories (fitting NACE classification), as well as 5 geographical areas of the Italian territory (classified by Istat). The dataset is composed by 30 main variables, mostly categorical indicators and some continuous variables, including firms' characteristics and processes, adoption of food waste practices, and food waste performances. The paper describes the methodology adopted for data collection and cleaning and presents some descriptive statistics. The main contribution of this work consists in providing the scientific community with an extensive dataset on a scarcely investigated and very relevant topic, with a high level of detail (firm-level data) and richness of variables. The dataset includes information on the quantity of surplus and waste produced, on the measurement process of these quantities, and on the valorization practices adopted for their management. These data are representative of the Italian food transformation sector and might enable and encourage further studies on the topic. The paper also provides the information needed for understanding the methodological steps adopted and to guide the interpretation of the results, to enable further studies based on the dataset.

metadata.title: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 34: When Personalization Becomes Pressure
metadata.description:
This white paper examines the shift in AI-powered personalization from relevance toward behavioral influence. Traditional personalization focused on understanding what customers want through declared preferences, transaction history, and observed behavior. Advanced AI systems increasingly infer what will make an individual act, including which message, offer, timing, incentive, price, or sequence is most likely to influence a decision. The paper argues that this transition changes personalization from a recommendation capability into an influence system requiring explicit enterprise governance.

The analysis distinguishes four personalization states: Recognition, Prediction, Persuasion, and Pressure. It further differentiates Assistive, Persuasive, Extractive, and Coercive personalization based on whether customer data primarily reduces effort, increases response, maximizes economic capture, or impairs meaningful choice. The paper identifies six factors that increase personalization pressure: Data Intimacy, Inference Opacity, Decision Stakes, Urgency Pressure, Choice Asymmetry, and Frequency.

Three case studies examine different manifestations of this governance problem. Instacart illustrates how algorithmic price experimentation becomes a customer fairness and regulatory issue once customers perceive price differences as personal. Meta demonstrates the relationship between consent design, economic terms, and meaningful customer choice. SHEIN illustrates how recommendation, engagement rewards, scarcity mechanics, and adaptive journeys raise system-level questions about customer agency and influence.

The paper introduces four original management frameworks. The Personalization Pressure Index provides a weighted diagnostic for assessing aggregate customer pressure. The Personalization Permission Ladder links deeper inference to stronger governance requirements. Trust-Adjusted Personalization Value incorporates the commercial cost of damaged trust into personalization economics. The Personalization Control Plane creates an authority layer between customer data and customer influence, covering data purpose, inferred information, influence intensity, pricing, frequency, human escalation, and customer override.

The central proposition is that maximum personalization should not be the enterprise objective. Sustainable personalization requires relevance aligned with customer benefit, explicit limits on behavioral authority, transparent use of consequential inferences, customer agency, and measurement of trust alongside conversion. The mature enterprise distinguishes between what AI is technically able to infer and what the business has earned permission to use.

 

Originally published on LoganSivanasen.com on 1 September 2026.

metadata.title: Особливості концепції "безпечної третьої країни" та її вплив на права дітей-мігрантів
metadata.description:
Постановка проблеми. Концепція "безпечної третьої країни" пройшла довгий шлях еволюції у праві ЄС. Вперше концепція виникла у зв’язку з прийняттям Дублінської Конвенції 1990 року та розвитком політики надання притулку в державах-членах ЄС. Закріпивши дану концепцію у Дублінській Конвенції, держави-члени ЄС зберегли за собою право відповідно до національного законодавства направляти особу, яка клопоче про надання притулку, до третьої країни. Сьогодні ця концепція визначена у Директиві 2013/32/ЄС та у Пакті про міграцію та притулок 2024 року. При цьому третя безпечна країна має дотримуватися міжнародних стандартів із прав людини у сфері притулку, встановлених міжнародно-правовими актами універсального та регіонального характеру, включаючи норми про заборону тортур, нелюдського чи такого, що принижує гідність, поводження чи покарання; дотримуватися міжнародних принципів стосовно захисту біженців, передбачених Конвенцією про статус біженців 1951 року і Протоколом щодо статусу біженців 1967 року, та стосовно осіб, які потребують додаткового захисту. Мета статті – визначити основні етапи розвитку концепції "безпечна третя країна" у праві ЄС та проаналізувати її вплив на права дітей-мігрантів. Методи: 1) діалектичний метод пізнання  дозволив дослідити еволюцію концепції "безпечної третьої країни", зміни в законодавстві ЄС і їхній вплив на права мігрантів, зокрема дітей; 2) історико-правовий метод дослідження дозволив простежити розвиток концепції у різних нормативних актах, від Дублінської Конвенції 1990 року до Пакту про міграцію та притулок 2024 року; 3) аналіз та синтез дозволив структурувати матеріал, зокрема, для розгляду елементів впливу концепції "безпечної третьої країни" на права дітей-мігрантів, а також для узагальнення результатів дослідження. Результати. Дублінські Регламенти призвели до того, що розподіл біженців відбувається нерівномірно. До того ж, застосування концепції "безпечної третьої країни" негативно впливає на права дітей-мігрантів, адже застосування цієї концепції іноді призводить до того, що діти часто вирішують продовжити свою небезпечну подорож до інших країн ЄС. Таким чином, через відсутність документів багато хто буде наражатися на ризики, включаючи насильство та експлуатацію з боку контрабандистів людей. Висновки. Концепція "безпечної третьої країни" в праві ЄС еволюціонувала від Дублінської Конвенції 1990 року до Пакту про міграцію та притулок 2024 року, і потребує подальшого вдосконалення для належного захисту дітей-мігрантів, враховуючи ризики в перевантажених системах прийому.

Problem statement. The concept of a "safe third country" has undergone a significant evolution in EU law. It first emerged with the adoption of the 1990 Dublin Convention and the development of asylum policies in EU Member States. By embedding this concept in the Dublin Convention, EU Member States retained the right, under national legislation, to transfer an asylum seeker to a third country. Today, the concept is defined in Directive 2013/32/EU and in the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum. A third safe country must adhere to international human rights standards in asylum matters, as established by international legal instruments of both universal and regional character. This includes prohibitions against torture, inhumane or degrading treatment or punishment, as well as compliance with international refugee protection principles enshrined in the 1951 Refugee Convention and the 1967 Refugee Protocol. Additionally, such a country must have national legislation on asylum and refugees, with its relevant authorities responsible for determining refugee status and granting asylum. Purpose. The purpose of this article is to identify the key stages in the development of the "safe third country" concept in EU law and analyze its impact on the rights of migrant children. Methods: 1) The dialectical method of cognition was used to explore the evolution of the "safe third country" concept, changes in EU legislation, and their impact on migrant rights, particularly those of children; 2) the historical-legal research method allowed for tracing the development of the concept in various legal acts, from the 1990 Dublin Convention to the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum; 3) analysis and synthesis structured the material, particularly in reviewing the elements of how the "safe third country" concept affects the rights of migrant children and summarizing the study's findings. Results. The Dublin Regulations led to an unequal distribution of refugees. Moreover, applying the "safe third country" concept negatively impacts migrant children's rights, as this policy often forces children to continue dangerous journeys to other EU countries. Consequently, due to a lack of proper documentation, many children are exposed to risks, including violence and exploitation by human traffickers. Conclusions. The "safe third country" concept in EU law has evolved from the 1990 Dublin Convention to the 2024 Pact on Migration and Asylum, but it still requires further refinement to ensure adequate protection for migrant children, particularly in overburdened reception systems.

metadata.title: Cybercrime Against Women as Gender-Based Violence: Victims' Procedural Protection and Fair Trial Guarantees for the Accused
metadata.description:
This article examines cybercrime against women as a form of gender-based violence and analyzes its implications for victims’ rights and fair trial guarantees for the accused. With the expansion of digital technologies, traditional forms of violence have migrated to online spaces, including cyberstalking, cyberbullying, online defamation, and non-consensual dissemination of intimate images. These acts are persistent and transnational, often producing psychological and social damage comparable to physical violence. The study investigates how existing legal frameworks struggle to respond effectively to abuse while simultaneously preserving fair trial guarantees and due process rights.

Using a doctrinal legal methodology, the research analyzes national legislation, European Union directives, and international instruments, including CEDAW and the Budapest Convention on Cybercrime, together with case law and academic literature. The findings reveal a structural imbalance in current legal systems. Victims often face secondary victimization through repeated interrogations, disclosure of private information, media exposure, and prolonged proceedings, which undermine their dignity, privacy, and participation in justice processes. At the same time, accused persons face risks to fair trial rights arising from media trials, public shaming, pre-trial assumptions of guilt, overbroad criminalization, intrusive digital investigations, and reliance on digital evidence whose reliability and integrity are often contested.

The article concludes that existing laws do not adequately protect either victims or the accused due to fragmented definitions of cyberviolence, technological gaps in evidence, jurisdictional challenges, and limited institutional capacity. It argues that victim protection and fair trial rights are complementary obligations.

metadata.title: Artifical intelligence and the challenges to legal regulation
metadata.description: The aim of this paper is to provide a brief history of the emergence and trends in the development of Artificial Intelligence, presenting in general terms its practical, economic and social significance and justifying the reasons that have necessitated the adoption of legal regulation within the European Union. The article briefly presents the scope of legal regulation and the main legal trends, as well as the objectives set by the new legal framework, while expressing reservations about the quality of the regulation, given that new legal institutes are being created for the first time and new social relations are being regulated for the first time, and the maturity of the regulation is to be tested in the course of law enforcement and future disputes that will inevitably arise. In the preparation of the paper, scientific methods such as desk research, comparative legal analysis and methods of legal interpretation have been used.

metadata.title: THE ISSUE OF INTRODUCING A COMPENSATORY INTEREST PAYMENT MECHANISM FOR THE REFUND OF OVERPAID OR COLLECTED CUSTOMS PAYMENTS
metadata.description: The article examines the current legal mechanism in the Republic of Uzbekistan for refunding overpaid or excessively collected customs payments and the issue arising from the absence of interest on refunded amounts. The temporary deprivation of an entrepreneur’s use of funds due to a customs authority’s error, unjustified additional assessment, or a subsequently revoked decision is assessed from the perspective of the time value of money. A comparative analysis of the practices of the United States, the Republic of Korea, Canada and the European Union is conducted, and a differentiated compensatory interest mechanism is proposed for Uzbekistan. In particular, the article substantiates charging compensatory interest from the date of payment or collection where the overpayment resulted from the fault of the customs authority, and, in other cases, for the period of delay in executing a refund decision, with the daily rate linked to 1/300 of the Central Bank refinancing rate.

metadata.title: The 2026 AI Inflection Series, Chapter 26: Your AI Agent Signed the Contract. Who Is Liable?
metadata.description:
This white paper examines the legal and commercial consequences of autonomous AI agents negotiating terms, accepting agreements, issuing purchase orders, accessing services, executing trades, and triggering contractual performance on behalf of enterprises. The paper argues that an AI agent rarely becomes the legal party to a transaction. External responsibility instead begins with attribution to the organisation whose systems, credentials, permissions, infrastructure, and commercial identity enabled the action.

The analysis distinguishes a technology agent from a legal agent and explains why autonomous software does not require independent legal personality before its actions create consequences for the deploying enterprise. Contract formation increasingly depends on attributable conduct, including automated acceptance messages, API execution, payment, repeated service use, delivery, and performance, rather than handwritten signatures or continuous human review.

Three legal cases, Chwee Kin Keong v Digilandmall.com, Register.com v Verio, and B2C2 v Quoine, illustrate principles of attribution, assent through automated conduct, and the enforceability of autonomously executed transactions. The paper synthesises these principles into a Seven-Layer Liability Architecture covering attribution, actual authority, apparent authority, assent through conduct, ratification and benefit, misrepresentation and reliance, and supply-chain and regulatory liability.

The paper also proposes a Nine-Layer Agentic Contract Control System covering purpose, legal entity, identity, authority envelope, terms and assent controls, pre-execution validation, runtime guardrails, contract observability, and stop, recovery, and reversal mechanisms. A seven-tier contracting risk model links increasing autonomous authority to stronger governance requirements while reserving acquisitions, borrowing, equity issuance, material guarantees, unlimited liability, restricted-party transactions, and other high-consequence commitments for human decision.

The central proposition is that machine autonomy does not absorb contractual responsibility. Enterprises remain accountable for defining where agent authority begins, where it ends, which events constitute assent, which terms agents are permitted to accept, and which evidence supports every material commitment.

metadata.description: This article analyzes the transformation of the civil liability framework regarding compensation for harm caused by artificial intelligence (AI) systems and autonomous algorithms to human life, health, property, and intangible rights. Current tort legislation is scrutinized through the lens of AI autonomy and algorithmic opacity. Drawing on a comparative legal approach, the paper examines modern practices and judicial case law from the European Union and the United States. The study concludes with practical and scholarly proposals for national legislation: categorizing high-risk AI systems as sources of increased danger, delineating liability between developers and operators, and introducing a rebuttable presumption of causality.

metadata.title: A report on recommendations for the most suitable financial contribution model for the Distributed System of Scientific Collections Research Infrastructure (DiSSCo-RI)
metadata.description:
A key consideration during the preparatory phase project DiSSCo Prepare – which laid the foundations for the future Research Infrastructure DiSSCo (Distributed System of Scientific Collections) – was the need to establish a small number of alternative viable financial contribution models and a scalable formula which could be presented to potential funders, with a view to obtaining the minimum financial contribution necessary for DiSSCo to operate, as well as considering how the RI could grow with increased national funding.

This report briefly explains the ERIC funding framework – as chosen for DiSSCo – and its legal constraints, in order to explain the key role played by national member contributions in the viability of an ERIC. An essential annex of the statutes that will be signed by all members of the ERIC is the member fee calculation. A proposal for the DiSSCo member fee calculation is set out in this document and is based on three main indicators: economic power (GDP), annual spending in research and development and population size. In the context of DiSSCo – and to ensure the ERIC can function – these indicators are connected to a fixed baseline fee of €50,000, in order to guarantee a minimum significant annual contribution from each participating country and avoid contributions that will be more expensive to manage than to benefit from. This baseline is multiplied by contribution factors which propose different ways to weight the various indicators.

The method is established on an ideal scenario, whereby all 27 EU members, as well as the UK, Iceland, Norway and Switzerland sign the DiSSCo statutes and agree to the proposed member contribution calculation, amounting to €4.5 million for the annual budget of the ERIC. This scenario remains highly unlikely; therefore, a scaled approach has been envisaged, meaning the initial engagement of some countries will allow DiSSCo to begin its operation and implement its business strategy, whilst the growth of the ERIC and its activities is likely to evolve proportionally to the number of national members it is able to engage.

This report also looks at the ways in which funding could be distributed amongst the DiSSCo members in order to implement decentralised services.

metadata.title: bulletin-fetcher: A Python library for programmatic access to EU official bulletins
metadata.description: EU Official Journal acts can be queried through public semantic web infrastructure, but using the underlying SPARQL endpoint requires knowledge of RDF vocabularies, query structure and EUR-Lex metadata conventions and ontologies. The bulletin-fetcher library abstracts this complexity behind a simple Python interface. Users can retrieve Official Journal acts by publication date, date ranges, act type, publishing institution and textual content, while receiving Python objects, JSON-compatible dictionaries, XML, CSV outputs or pandas DataFrames suitable for further analysis.

metadata.title: EU Digital Identity Wallet: Legal, Regulatory, and Compliance Risks under eIDAS 2.0, GDPR, and the AI Act
metadata.description: This framework provides a consolidated legal, regulatory, and policy analysis of the European Digital Identity Wallet under Regulation (EU) 2024/1183 (eIDAS 2.0). It integrates GDPR, the Charter of Fundamental Rights, the AI Act, CJEU jurisprudence, the Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2, the Data Act, the European Health Data Space, the Digital Services Act, the Digital Markets Act, the Anti-Money Laundering Regulation, the Interchange Fee Regulation, and the proposed Legal Tender Regulation. The 2026 update incorporates verified corrections on AI liability, biometric-governance scope, and cash‑acceptance obligations following the European Parliament ECON Committee vote of 23 June 2026. It identifies five systemic risks recurring across Member State implementations: de facto compulsion; cross-sector linkage and profiling; fragmented accountability; weak data minimisation; and payment-choice erosion. The framework explains how these risks interact with concurrent EU reforms, including the Digital Omnibus package and the revised AI Act compliance deadlines. It provides a regulatory red‑flag checklist, verified sourcing notes, and strategic mitigation recommendations for legislators, regulators, and relying parties. A consolidated legislative horizon summarises all fixed deadlines and pending files relevant to digital identity, payments, cybersecurity, and platform governance.
